Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened

Vignette:
Amir was twenty years old when it happened, a junior auditor who still felt the giddy relief of having landed a good job straight out of community college. His ex-boyfriend—a man he had trusted, whose apartment he had visited dozens of times—invited him over one evening to “talk things through” after their breakup. Amir remembered the smell of the place: the specific cologne his ex always wore, layered over the faint must of old carpet and the sharpness of the takeout they had ordered. He remembered thinking that maybe they could salvage something, that this conversation might ease the ache of the split. Instead, his ex became angry, then coercive, then violent. By the time it was over, Amir had been raped in that apartment, on that familiar couch, with the cologne still clinging to his shirt and the words “you owe me this” still ringing in his ears.

For weeks afterward, Amir could not bring himself to talk about it. He went to work, sat at his desk, and stared at spreadsheets while his mind replayed fragments. The smell of cologne anywhere—on a coworker, in an elevator, even in a department store—would make his stomach clench and his vision narrow. He began to avoid the men’s grooming aisle entirely. At first, he dismissed these reactions as temporary. But the world kept reminding him. A colleague made a crude joke about someone “deserving what they got,” and Amir felt a hot shame rise in his chest, as though the comment were aimed directly at him. He heard a friend say, “I would never put up with that,” and his internal response was automatic: *Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation. I should have known better.* The humiliation settled into him like a low-grade fever, persistent and corrosive.

Over the following months, Amir’s life contracted. He had always been a careful, detail-oriented person—an asset at work—but now that precision became a cage. He stopped accepting invitations to parties or group dinners because he could not assess the risk of unfamiliar locations. Any new restaurant or bar felt like a trap; he needed to know the layout, the exits, the escape routes before he could even consider stepping inside. At the office, he learned to map the floor plan of every conference room he entered, always choosing a seat with a clear path to the door. His body stayed on alert: a sudden movement from a coworker reaching for a stapler would make him flinch; footsteps behind him in the hallway would make his shoulders lock. He stopped wearing the fitted shirts he used to like, instead opting for loose, dark hoodies that made him feel less visible, less likely to draw anyone’s attention.

The hardest part was at work. Auditing required periodic performance evaluations, and Amir dreaded them. He began to dread any situation in which someone might evaluate his appearance, his work, or his presence. He would slip into meetings late and leave early, keeping his voice low, avoiding eye contact. When his supervisor scheduled a quarterly review, Amir felt the familiar surge of dread—not about the numbers, but about being seen, being judged, being trapped in a room with someone who could say anything. He started calling in sick on review days, then taking personal days, then fabricating excuses. His productivity did not suffer—the work itself was solitary and he did it well—but his relationship with his team grew distant. Colleagues who once invited him for coffee stopped; they assumed he was cold or unfriendly.

What kept him awake at night was the sense that the person he had been was gone. He remembered being a happy kid, the one who made his family laugh, who looked forward to weekends with friends. Now he felt hollow and irritable, unable to access that version of himself. The world felt dangerous, and he felt marked. When anyone said something that reminded him of his ex—a phrase, a tone of voice—he would feel the floor drop out from under him.

It was after a third missed performance review that his boss gently suggested he speak with someone. Amir agreed, partly because he was exhausted and partly because he was afraid of losing the one stable thing he had left. He walked into the therapist’s office and sat in the chair closest to the door, his hoodie pulled tight around him, and waited for someone to tell him whether he could survive telling the whole story. What he wanted most was to stop feeling humiliated. What he feared most was that the humiliation had become part of who he was.
